response:
ACCEPT.The new theorem is valid under its stated hypotheses. The pinwheel deduction, the exact mixed-export count, the directed-path argument for arbitrarily many bands, the even-length improvement, the joint accounting, and the uniform sharp family all work. The receiver application correctly requires closure at the whole-packet level, using the original single-terminal receiver ledger supplied in the dependency.I found no substantive mathematical gap. This verdict concerns the written proof and constructions; it does not certify the reported finite-control totals or any Lean execution.1. The native witnesses force both TP columns and the opposite BB columnsConsider the displayed crossing edge
$$u=(1,c),\qquad v=(2,c),$$
with bands in rows  $\{0,1\}$  and  $\{2,3\}$ .Let  $L_u,L_v\subseteq\{-1,+1\}$  record which lateral neighbors of the respective endpoints are selected. Each endpoint has only three nonmate neighbors: its outer vertical neighbor and its two lateral neighbors. Consequently, the requirement of at least two original selected neighbors implies
$$L_u\ne\varnothing,\qquad L_v\ne\varnothing.$$
These sets are disjoint. If both  $(1,c+\varepsilon)$  and  $(2,c+\varepsilon)$  were selected, the upper selection would have two occupied neighbors:  $u$  and the lower selection. This violates feasibility.Two nonempty disjoint subsets of a two-element set must therefore be opposite singletons. Each endpoint has exactly one lateral selection and must obtain its second selected witness from its outer vertical neighbor. Thus
$$(0,c),(3,c)\in T,$$
and both endpoints lie in TP columns.For the orientation in (3), the forced blanks are obtained exactly as claimed:Forced blankSelection that excludes occupation there $(0,c-1)$  $(0,c)$ , already adjacent to  $u$  $(1,c-1)$  $(2,c-1)$ , already adjacent to  $v$  $(2,c+1)$  $(1,c+1)$ , already adjacent to  $u$  $(3,c+1)$  $(3,c)$ , already adjacent to  $v$ Hence the upper-band column  $c-1$  is BB and the lower-band column  $c+1$  is BB. The reflected orientation reverses their roles.These exclusions forbid all occupation, including endpoints, because each excluding selection already has one occupied neighbor. This is precisely where the original-selected-witness hypothesis matters.The same argument gives the complete neighborhood of each endpoint: its mate, its two selected witnesses, and a blank fourth neighbor. Therefore neither endpoint has another endpoint neighbor, and the original endpoint component is an isolated  $K_2$ . Both endpoints already possess their native witnesses, so the asserted immediate freezing uses no retained endpoints or later freezing steps.Finally, a TP column cannot be either boundary column: the first is BB, and the last has a blank corner. Thus the internal-column assertion is justified.2. The export identity is exactly  $\sum_i e_i=2r$ Take any mixed export counted by  $e_i$ . Its TP endpoint has its mate outside  $I_i$ , but hypothesis 1 places that mate inside  $J$ .Because the TP column is internal to the common column interval, this matching edge cannot leave the band horizontally through a column end. It must cross the horizontal boundary into an adjacent band. It is therefore one of the charged edges.Conversely, the pinwheel argument proves that both ends of every charged edge are TP endpoints. Such an edge contributes exactly one mixed-export incidence to each of its two bands.Consequently,
$$\sum_i e_i=2r.$$
There is no omitted contribution from nonmixed matching edges. An internal or external matching edge involving only BP or PP endpoint columns contributes nothing to the  $e_i$ , while its endpoint weight remains included in the regional balances and the strip identities.3. The joined graph is a directed-path forest for arbitrary numbers of bandsThe dependency’s BB–TT forest has the required interval structure. Every TT column has two BB neighbors and cannot occur at either boundary. Each connected component is therefore a contiguous alternating interval
$$\mathrm{BB},\mathrm{TT},\ldots,\mathrm{TT},\mathrm{BB},$$
including the possibility of a singleton BB. Its length is odd.Adjacent BB columns without an intervening TT are separate components. This does not cause a problem: each component is still a well-defined interval, and every BB or TT column belongs to exactly one such component.For a charged edge at column  $c$ , let its source and destination intervals be
$$[a,b]\quad\text{and}\quad[a',b'].$$
The forced BB columns and the TP columns at  $c$  give the exact equalities
$$b=c-1,\qquad a'=c+1=b+2.$$
The degree bounds follow from these exact endpoint positions:An outgoing edge from an interval ending at  $b$  must use the TP column  $b+1$  in that interval’s band.That column has exactly one endpoint.That endpoint has exactly one actual mate.Thus the outdegree is at most one. The corresponding argument at the column immediately before the interval’s left endpoint gives indegree at most one.This remains valid for an interior band with neighboring bands on both sides: its relevant TP column still contains only one endpoint, so it cannot supply two different actual matching edges across those two boundaries.Every directed edge strictly increases column position. Therefore directed cycles are impossible. With indegree and outdegree at most one, an undirected cycle would necessarily be a directed cycle: every vertex on it would need one incoming and one outgoing edge. Hence no undirected cycle exists either.The graph is consequently a disjoint union of directed paths and isolated vertices. Distinct charged edges cannot give parallel copies of one connection, because that would already violate the unique-mate argument at its source.There are exactly  $F$  interval vertices and  $r$  graph edges, so
$$h=F-r.$$
This argument counts each interval once and applies to arbitrary finite  $k$ . It requires neither planarity nor a separate global injection of physical donors.4. The first-column sources and sealed final sinks give  $h\ge k+t$ Each band’s first-column BB belongs to an interval starting at the first column of  $J$ . Such an interval has no incoming edge. The  $k$  intervals are distinct because they belong to distinct bands.A directed path has exactly one source, so these  $k$  vertices lie on distinct paths. Thus
$$h\ge k.$$
For the even sealed improvement, the parity assertion is exact. Suppose a directed path has interval lengths
$$\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m.$$
Each  $\ell_j$  is odd, and each consecutive pair of intervals is separated by exactly one column. Its total column span is therefore
$$\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_m+(m-1).$$
Modulo two, this is
$$m+(m-1)\equiv1.$$
Every path has odd span, regardless of how often it changes bands.Each sealed final BB interval is a sink: an outgoing edge would require a TP column beyond the last column of  $J$ . The  $t$  such intervals lie on distinct paths because a directed path has only one sink.If one of these paths also contained a first-column source, it would start at the first column and end at the last, so its span would be  $n$ . This is impossible when  $n$  is even.The  $t$  sealed-sink paths are therefore distinct from all  $k$  first-source paths, proving
$$h\ge k+t.$$
Setting  $t=0$  for odd  $n$  is appropriate: the parity obstruction disappears, and an alternating interval can connect two blank boundary columns across an odd-length strip.5. The joint accounting is exactThe dependency supplies, in each band,
$$2S_{I_i}+e_i=2(B_i-A_i)+u_i,
\qquad
u_i=D_i-C_i+e_i\ge0.$$
Here  $u_i\ge0$  comes from the actual-mate injection into BP columns. It does not depend on treating endpoint adjacency as a substitute for matching.The bands partition  $J$ , so
$$S_J=\sum_i S_{I_i}.$$
Summing the strip identities and substituting the established export count gives
$$2S_J+2r=2F+U.$$
Using  $F-r=h$ ,
$$\boxed{S_J=h+\frac U2}.$$
Therefore
$$S_J\ge h\ge k+t.$$
This is the cancellation required by the theorem. The  $r$  units arising from the  $2r$  mixed-export incidences are absorbed by the difference between the number of interval vertices and the number of joined paths. No empty column is separately allocated to multiple exports, and no internal receiver fragment is added as a second resource.The matching formulation is also exactly equivalent:
$$|P\cap J|=2|M_{\rm in}|+a$$
gives

=kn-|T\cap J|-|M_{\rm in}|-\frac a2.$$
Thus (1) and (2) are equivalent even when the permitted nonmixed matching edges cross the packet boundary.6. Union receiver closure then places the component’s entire physical receiver inside that packet.For pairwise tile-disjoint packets, each complete receiver therefore belongs either:wholly to one packet, orwholly to the exterior of all packets.It cannot meet two packets, since closure for either would place its complete receiver inside that packet.Using the original single-terminal component ledger from the dependency, the resulting split is exactly

A negative raw fragment in one band cannot also enter  $R_{\rm out}$ , and the note correctly avoids doing that.Also,  $D_{\rm out}\ge0$ . An endpoint-free original  $2\times2$  tile contains at most two selections: any three selected corners would give one of those selections two selected neighbors. Thus each such tile has nonnegative deficit  $2-|T\cap Q|$ .Consequently,
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
\ge
\sum_J(k_J+t_J)+D_{\rm out}-q+R_{\rm out},$$
and the stated sufficient condition
$$q\le\sum_J(k_J+t_J)$$
indeed proves the global half-area bound.Individual bands need no receiver closure. Their signed fragments can cancel within the exact packet balance. Rotated packets cause no additional ownership issue provided they remain unions of original physical tiles and are tile-disjoint, as required.7.
